I always wake up at sunrise to practise bokator with my grandfather at his bokator club. He is very skilled at bokator, he was once a very good fighter who hardly ever lost a fight. He is very strict, he often tells me to work harder, and he hardly ever says “good job!” At 12:30, I leave for school. I usually run to school, but I sometimes walk when I feel lazy. Lyvann:
I usually wake up at five o’clock. I sometimes wake up late when I stay up at night reading a book
or looking at the stars. But I always get to school early—before 6:30—because, as Class Monitor, it is my job to make sure the students clean the classroom before school starts. I am never late, and the classroom is always clean when Ms. Mom arrives.
After school, I always stay for extra lessons, usually until noon or one o’clock.
I always stop at the photocopy shop on my way home, because as Class Monitor, it is my job to make copies of the exercises for class the next day. In the afternoon, I go to my family’s pharmacy to help out. It isn’t usually very busy, so I often practise playing a traditional instrument I play, called a kloy.

Pisey:
I usually wake up at 6 o’clock. I never eat breakfast; instead, I sleep late. I hardly ever
walk to school, because I’m too lazy. My brother usually brings me to school on his bicycle.
I often get bored at school because I’m so smart and I know everything already. But I always enjoy dance class. I am an amazing dancer, so the teacher often asks me to help my classmates learn new steps.
When school ends at 11 o’clock, I always go to the market where my family sells clothing and eat lunch with my Mum. After lunch, I stay at
the market to sell clothes. I always earn a lot of money, because I know so much about fashion. After I finish at the market, I often go to learn traditional dance.
Then I go home and eat dinner with my family.

THE PLURAL POEM

We’ll begin with a box, and the plural is boxes;
But the plural of ox should be oxen not oxes.
One fowl is a goose, but two are called geese,
Yet the plural of moose should never be meese.

You may find a lone mouse or a nest full of mice,
But the plural of house is houses, not hice.
If the plural of man is always called men,
Why shouldn’t the plural of pan be called pen?

If I spoke of my foot and showed you my feet,
When I give you a boot, would a pair be called beet?
If one is a tooth and a whole set are teeth,
Why shouldn’t the plural of booth be called beeth?

If the singular is this, and the plural is these,
Why shouldn’t the plural of kiss be kese?
Then one may be that, and three would be those,
Yet the plural of hat would never be hose.

We speak of a brother and also of brethren,
But though we say mother, we never say methren.
So plurals in English, I think you’ll agree,
Are indeed very tricky--singularly.
--Anonymous

You’re wearing your squeaky shoes

Is a tiger, so how do you walk on by?
Silently ... silently ... silent L-Y
You’re a secret agent man
Who’s after the secret plan
How do you act so they don’t know you’re as spy?
Normally, normally, normal L-Y
At an eating contest you boast
That you can eat the most
How do you down your fiftieth piece of pie? Eagerly, eagerly, eager L-Y
On the lake your boat upset
And your clothes got soaking wet
How do you stand and wait for them to dry? D-d-d patiently, d-d-d patiently, patient L-Y In the public library
You fall and you hurt your knee
But the sign says, “quiet please,” so how can you cry?
Quietly, quietly, quiet L-Y
As you walk along the street
A porcupine you meet
How do you shake his hand when he says hi? Carefully, carefully, careful L-Y
You enter a very dark room
And sitting there in the gloom
Is Dracula! Now how do you say goodbye? Immediately, immediately, immediate L-Y Bye Bye!
